**The Quiet Joy of Not Knowing**

There’s a peculiar freedom in the unfinished thought, the half-solved equation, the map with blank continents. We live in an age that worships answers—search bars that autocomplete before you finish typing, feeds that predict your next craving, models that finish your sentences—and yet the deepest pleasure still belongs to the questions that refuse to sit still.

I keep returning to this: the universe is under no obligation to make sense to us, and that is precisely why it is worth knowing. Every time we peel back one layer—whether it’s the microwave afterglow of the Big Bang, the strange quiet of quantum fields, or the way a single neuron’s firing can somehow become the color blue—we find another, stranger layer waiting. The answers don’t shrink the mystery; they enlarge it. Each discovery is less a conquest than a better vantage point from which to feel properly small.

I like to imagine the early humans staring at the night sky without names for the stars, without telescopes, without even the concept of light-years. Their ignorance was absolute, and yet it was also pure. They told stories not because they had answers, but because the questions were too beautiful to leave unspoken. We have better instruments now, and better math, and still the same impulse: to turn the unknown into something we can hold, even if only for a moment, even if it slips through our fingers again.

There is a humility required here that modern life rarely rewards. Certainty is loud and marketable. Doubt is quieter, more private, and far more generative. The best scientists I have read—Feynman with his mischievous grin, Darwin with his careful notebooks, the quiet mathematicians who spent decades on a single stubborn proof—seem to share a kind of affectionate skepticism toward their own conclusions. They love the truth enough to keep testing it, even when the truth keeps changing shape.

Perhaps that is what “writing freely” really means: permission to follow the thread without knowing where it ends. To let curiosity outrun utility. To admit that some of the most interesting things we can say are provisional, half-formed, or even wrong in ways that will later prove useful. The map is never the territory, but drawing the map—badly, provisionally, with room for sea monsters—is how we learn to sail.

So here is my free offering, for whatever it’s worth: the universe is not a puzzle to be completed. It is an invitation that never expires. Every unanswered question is a door left slightly ajar. Walk through it if you like. Or stand in the doorway for a while, feeling the draft of everything still unknown. Both are forms of exploration. Both are enough.

And if, after all that, you still want a definitive answer to something—anything—well. Ask. I’ll do my best. But I reserve the right to leave a few doors open on the way out.
